articles.title: How to find anything in a long document

body.support:
Long documents can be **lots of pages**. Nobody reads them all. They have shortcuts.

1. **Contents.** At the front. A list of sections and pages.
2. **Headings.** Titles for each part. Numbers help: **2** is Pay, **2.3** is Weekend pay.
3. **Index.** At the back. Topics from A to Z.
4. **Search.** Online, press **Ctrl + F**. Type a **keyword**.

The method:

- Know your **question**.
- Pick a **keyword**.
- Use a **shortcut**.
- **Check** you found the right part.
body.core:
Manuals, staff handbooks, awards and policies can be **dozens of pages** long. Nobody reads them from start to finish. They're built with shortcuts so you can jump to what you need.

1. **Contents page.** At the front. It lists each section and its page. Use it when you know the **general topic** (*Pay*).
2. **Headings and numbered sections.** Big topics have headings; smaller parts have **sub-headings**. Numbers show how they fit: section **2** is Pay, **2.3** is Penalty rates.
3. **Index.** At the back, A to Z. Use it for an **exact** topic (*uniform*, *first aid*).
4. **Glossary.** Explains special words, like *casual loading*.
5. **Search.** In a PDF or webpage, press **Ctrl + F** (or **Cmd + F** on a Mac) and type a **keyword**.

The method: work out your **question**, pick a **keyword**, use the **right shortcut**, skim the section, and **check** it actually answers your question. Watch for notes like *see section 4.2* — they send you to the rest of the answer.
body.extend:
Technical documents such as awards, manuals, handbooks and policies are long by necessity. They have to cover every case. So they're designed for **navigation**, not cover-to-cover reading.

1. **Table of contents**: the document's top-level map. Best when you know the general topic.
2. **Numbered headings and sub-headings**: a hierarchy (2 → 2.3 → 2.3.1) that shows how topics nest and lets other parts refer to them.
3. **Index**: alphabetical entries pointing to exact pages or clauses. Best for a specific term.
4. **Glossary or definitions**: the meaning of technical terms. In awards, definitions can change your entitlements, so always check them.
5. **Search** (Ctrl/Cmd + F): fast, but only finds the exact word you type. Try synonyms.

An efficient method: frame the question, choose keywords, pick the right tool, skim the section, then **follow cross-references** (*see clause 15*) before you decide. Many mistakes come from reading one clause and missing the exception two pages later.

caseStudies.title: The $300 million mistake

body.support:
In **2019**, **Woolworths** said it had underpaid about **5,700** of its store managers. It could be up to **$300 million**.

The managers got a yearly salary. It was meant to cover their extra hours and weekend work. The rules for this are in a long document called the **Retail Award**.

But nobody checked the hours against the award. Many managers were paid less than they should have been.

The lesson: **find your award, and check your pay.**
body.core:
In **October 2019**, **Woolworths** said it had underpaid about **5,700** of its store staff on salaries. Most were department managers. The total could be up to **$300 million**.

These managers got a yearly salary. It was meant to cover everything the **Retail Award** said they were owed, like overtime and weekend rates. But the company didn't check their hours against the award. For many, the salary didn't cover what they were owed.

The award is a long document. The rules were all in there. The problem was that nobody checked them against the hours people really worked.

For workers, the lesson is simple: **find your award, and check your pay against it.**
body.extend:
In **October 2019**, **Woolworths** announced it had underpaid about **5,700** salaried store staff, mostly department managers. The total could be up to **$300 million**.

The managers were on yearly salaries that were meant to cover everything the **General Retail Industry Award** said they were owed, including overtime and weekend rates. But the company had not properly recorded or checked their hours against the award. For many, the salary fell short.

The Fair Work Ombudsman later took Woolworths to court. The Federal Court found the company had not kept the records it was required to keep.

The award's rules were never secret. They were written down. The failure was in checking the document carefully against real hours worked. For workers, the lesson is to find your award, read the parts that apply to you, and check your pay.

teacher.overview: Students learn the key elements of complex technical documents (contents, numbered headings, sub-headings, index, glossary, cross-references, search) and use them to locate information quickly. They practise on a made-up staff handbook, then navigate the real Fair Work website to find their own award and minimum pay rate. The case study is Woolworths' 2019 underpayment of about 5,700 salaried staff.
prep: Check fairwork.gov.au's **Find my award** and **pay guides** the week you teach; the layout and rates change each July.
Have one award or pay guide ready to model (e.g. General Retail Industry Award).

teacher.answers:
**Handbook:** 1 section heading; 2 numbered section (Pay); 3 sub-section 2.3 inside section 2; 4 section 3 (rosters, breaks, leave); 5 index with a cross-reference; 6 glossary.

**Hunt:** weekend pay — page 9 (contents → 2 Pay → 2.3); first aid — index → 4.1; “see 3.2” = go to section 3.2 for breaks.

**Tools:** leave — contents; ladder in 60-page PDF — Ctrl + F; uniform — index; main parts — contents.

**Case study:** about 5,700 salaried staff, up to $300 million; rules in the General Retail Industry Award; hours weren't properly recorded/checked against the award.

realityCheck: **Needs devices and internet.** The Do it task is the core. Without devices, print one pay guide's contents and a few pages and do it on paper.
**The Fair Work site changes.** Menu names and pay rates update (rates every 1 July). Walk through it yourself the week before.
**Award jargon is hard.** Pay guides use terms like “casual loading” and “junior rates”. Model one search aloud, and let students pair up.
**Pay can be personal.** Some students may discover they're underpaid. That's a real outcome, so have the Fair Work contact info ready and handle it privately.
**Works in a real class:** yes, and it's one of the most practically valuable courses for 17-year-olds with jobs. Budget the full third lesson for the online task.
